problem: Visual navigation foundation models (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD) predict waypoints normalized by the average training step size, but at deployment the physical step size is unknown and cannot be inferred from images alone. Changing speed or control frequency distorts trajectory geometry, causing collisions. These models also struggle in visually repetitive, featureless scenes.
motivation: Zero-shot cross-embodiment deployment needs metric-aligned waypoints that stay robust to robot speed and control frequency. The same visual change can come from a fast robot slowing down or a slow robot at full speed, so vision alone leaves the scale ambiguous. Past normalized actions act like a baseline in multi-view geometry and give the scale reference.
key_idea: Condition a DINOv3-based navigation transformer on the normalized action history so it can relate observed visual displacement to physical step size and predict metric-aligned normalized waypoints.
insight: The offline cross-track test shows the DINOv3 encoder gives most of the scale consistency (VISTA w/o AH is slightly better on cross-track error), while action history gives lower action and distance loss. In the real world, w/o AH collides in 5/5 Office-Lab trials, and the full model succeeds 5/5, so action history matters for tight-turn control under velocity variation. ViNT fails at low step sizes while VISTA copes with them, and conditioning in normalized action space avoids a metric-to-normalized grounding problem.
method: DINOv3 ViT-S tokenization: observation and goal images (192x192) are encoded into patch tokens, projected with 2x pixel-unshuffle downsampling, with a 0.1x learning-rate multiplier on the encoder.
Action-history conditioning: past k-1 displacements normalized by the step size (a_i = Δp_i/φ) are encoded by an MLP into tokens of the same dimension and fed to the transformer.
Transformer decoder: 6 layers, 512 dim, 8 heads, with readout tokens for distance and action, learnable temporal embeddings, and 2D RoPE on patch tokens; 42M parameters in total.

Normalized metric training: the step size is computed per trajectory (average waypoint spacing) and used to normalize waypoints; the distance head regresses normalized metric distance instead of temporal distance (so negative sampling is dropped); loss = λ L_action + μ(1-λ) L_dist with λ=0.5, μ=0.01.
Varied spacing training: dataset sampling frequency is varied from 2 to 12 Hz to train robustness to different speeds and control frequencies.
Deployment: topological-map navigation with a windowed closest-node search, denormalization by v_max/f, and waypoint index 1 with radius 2.

setting.backbone: DINOv3 ViT-S + 6-layer transformer (trained; DINO fine-tuned at 0.1x LR)
setting.training_data: GoStanford, RECON, SACSoN, SCAND and TartanDrive trajectories (roughly 86 h in total), resampled at 2-12 Hz; RGB only
setting.observation: monocular RGB (fisheye) context sequence + goal image + past normalized action history; odometry from LiDAR (SuperOdometry) for the action history
setting.action_space: predicted normalized 2D waypoints (horizon 5), denormalized by v_max/f_ctrl and tracked by a controller
setting.simulator: real world only (offline evaluation on datasets)
setting.privileged: pre-collected topological map of goal images from a manual reference traversal; odometry poses for action history

numbers_note: No standard benchmark is used. Results are custom real-world trials (Outdoor 3 trials, Forest 5, Office-Lab 5) and offline losses, reported as counts rather than SR/SPL. The PTN and path-length figures are only in figures.
results: In zero-shot real-world trials VISTA succeeded in 3/3 Outdoor, 5/5 Forest and 5/5 Office-Lab, with about 95% of checkpoints crossed on average. ViNT, NoMaD and MetricNet suffered collisions or false goal predictions, and VISTA w/o AH collided in 5/5 Office-Lab trials. Offline, VISTA had the lowest distance loss (3.595 vs ViNT 11.581) and action loss (0.217 vs 0.589) and lower cross-track error than ViNT and NoMaD.
limitations: No knowledge of robot geometry or traversability, so it can fail where embodiment matters (e.g. stairs).
It struggles when consecutive observations are near-identical in visually similar scenes.
It degrades at very low control frequency (≤1 Hz); real-world trial counts are small (3-5 per setting).
